title: HEMORRHAGIC DESTRUCTION OF THE BRAIN, SUBEPENDYMAL CALCIFICATION, AND CATARACTS

relationships.phenotype: HEMORRHAGIC DESTRUCTION OF THE BRAIN, SUBEPENDYMAL CALCIFICATION, AND CATARACTS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts (HDBSCC) is caused by homozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene on chromosome 11q25.

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts (HDBSCC) is caused by homozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous mutation in the tight-junction protein JAM3 causes hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts.

checks.claim: The JAM3 gene is located on chromosome 11q25.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygosity mapping identified the disease locus in this family on chromosome 11q25 with a maximum multipoint LOD score of 6.15. Sequence analysis of genes in the candidate interval uncovered a mutation in the canonical splice-donor site of intron 5 of JAM3.
checks.explanation: JAM3 lies in the 11q25 candidate interval.

paragraphs.text: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Affected individuals have congenital cataracts and severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain with subependymal calcification (Mochida et al., 2010). Akawi et al. (2013) described the neonatal course as catastrophic, and most affected children died in the first weeks of life.

paragraphs.text: Mochida et al. (2010) studied 8 affected members of a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates. All affected individuals had hemorrhagic destruction of the brain parenchyma, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts. Mochida et al. (2010) noted that the clinical picture overlapped with some reported cases of pseudo-TORCH syndrome and with patients who have mutations in occludin, another tight-junction component. However, the massive intracranial hemorrhage set these patients apart. In a later summary of this family, Akawi et al. (2013) stated that 3 of the 8 affected individuals died early in infancy. They also stated that brain imaging showed multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhage with liquefaction and massive cystic degeneration, resulting in large ventricles.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) reported affected children from 3 families of different ethnic origin. In family 1, the parents were Turkish second cousins. Their first child was a preterm girl who had intracranial bleeding and died in the neonatal period. The second child was a girl born at term with a birth weight of 2480 gm (less than 10th centile). On day 5 she was admitted with tonic seizures that did not respond to treatment. Examination showed a head circumference of 30 cm, a sloping forehead, a prominent, bulging anterior fontanel, bitemporal grooving, and bilateral nuclear cataracts. Brain CT showed calcification of the subependymal region and multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Tests for toxoplasmosis, rubella, and cytomegalovirus were negative, and the platelet count was normal. She developed posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus and died at 2 months of age.

paragraphs.text: In family 2 of Akawi et al. (2013), the parents were nonconsanguineous and of Afghani origin. The first affected boy had bilateral cataracts and feeding problems from birth. At 2 weeks of age he developed vomiting, irritability, and a high-pitched cry. Brain MRI at 15 days showed grade IV intraventricular hemorrhage, severe ventricular dilatation, white matter abnormalities, and multiple subependymal cysts. Renal ultrasound showed horseshoe kidneys. He died at 2 weeks of age, and extensive metabolic, mitochondrial, cytogenetic, and coagulation studies were normal. His affected brother had bilateral cataracts at birth. Cranial ultrasound at first showed periventricular echogenicity without bleeding. On day 5 his hemoglobin fell from 180 to 96 g/L, and repeat ultrasound showed extensive bilateral intracerebral hemorrhage. EEG had shown bilateral epileptiform activity, and abdominal ultrasound showed right pelvicalyceal dilatation. He died on the fifth day of life.

paragraphs.text: In family 3 of Akawi et al. (2013), the parents were Moroccan first cousins. Earlier, a male child had died at 10 days of age with cerebral hemorrhage and hydrocephalus, and a stillborn child had hydrocephalus with necrotic degeneration of the cerebral tissue. The index patient was a girl with central and nuclear bilateral cataracts at birth. On the second day of life she had irritability and a bulging anterior fontanel. Head CT showed multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhages, subependymal calcification, and diffusely hypodense brain parenchyma. MRI showed intraventricular and intraparenchymal hemorrhage, edema, cystic changes, dilated ventricles, and a thin corpus callosum. The circulation in the circle of Willis was normal. EEG showed electrical status epilepticus, but she had no clinical seizures. She also had severe anemia. Metabolic screening and platelet levels were normal. By day 18 her head circumference was 41 cm (+4 SD), and she died at 39 days of age.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) found that the phenotype in their patients was very similar to that in the original family. All of their patients had bilateral cataracts and intraparenchymal hemorrhage with brain destruction and calcification. Renal anomalies and liver enlargement varied more between patients. The authors reported that the disorder was lethal in 7 of 10 cases, with death in the first few weeks of life. The 3 survivors had severe mental retardation, severe spasticity, and seizures.

paragraphs.text: Mochida et al. (2010) studied affected members of a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates. They sequenced the 9 protein-coding genes in the candidate interval on 11q25 and found a homozygous mutation in the canonical splice donor site of intron 5 of the JAM3 gene (c.747+1G-T). The change was predicted to abolish the normal splice donor site. RT-PCR analysis of a patient lymphoblastoid cell line confirmed abnormal splicing, which led to a frameshift with early termination.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) sequenced the coding exons of JAM3 in affected children from 3 families of Turkish, Afghani, and Moroccan origin. They found 3 different homozygous mutations: C219Y, E116K, and M1R. The mutations segregated with the disease. Parents were heterozygous, and unaffected sibs available for testing were either homozygous for the wildtype allele or heterozygous. None of the mutations was present in dbSNP or the 1000 Genomes Project. In transfected HeLa cells, the C219Y mutant protein was mostly retained in the endoplasmic reticulum. In contrast, the E116K mutant reached the plasma membrane normally, like wildtype JAM3.

checks.explanation: The families are Turkish, Afghani and Moroccan.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) discussed the differential diagnosis. The syndrome of band-like intracranial calcification with simplified gyration and polymicrogyria, caused by OCLN mutations, lacks intracranial hemorrhage and congenital cataract, and their patients had no polymicrogyria. Disorders caused by COL4A1 mutations can include antenatal intracranial hemorrhage and porencephaly, but they are inherited as autosomal dominant traits and present differently. Proliferative vasculopathy and hydranencephaly-hydrocephaly (Fowler syndrome), caused by FLVCR2 mutations, presents with fetal akinesia deformation sequence, which differs from HDBSCC.

checks.claim: The syndrome of band-like intracranial calcification with simplified gyration and polymicrogyria is caused by OCLN mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: the syndrome of band-like intracranial calcification, simplified cerebral gyrai and polymicrogyria. This syndrome is caused by mutations in another TJ gene, occludin (OCLN; MIM# 602876).

checks.claim: The syndrome of band-like intracranial calcification with simplified gyration and polymicrogyria lacks intracranial hemorrhage and congenital cataract.
checks.evidence_quote: However, patients with this syndrome do not have intracranial hemorrhage or congenital cataract.

checks.claim: The HDBSCC patients of Akawi et al. (2013) had no polymicrogyria.
checks.evidence_quote: our patients did not show any evidence of developmental malformation of the cerebral cortex and polymicrogyria

checks.claim: Disorders caused by COL4A1 mutations can include antenatal intracranial hemorrhage and porencephaly.
checks.evidence_quote: can cause overlapping clinical presentations which include antenatal intracranial hemorrhage, brain small vessel disease with hemorrhage or vascular leukoencephalopathy, porencephaly

checks.claim: Disorders caused by COL4A1 mutations are inherited as autosomal dominant traits and present differently from HDBSCC.
checks.evidence_quote: All these disorders are inherited as autosomal dominant and the clinical presentations is different from the cases in this report.

checks.claim: Proliferative vasculopathy and hydranencephaly-hydrocephaly (Fowler syndrome) is caused by FLVCR2 mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: It is caused by mutations in the FLVCR2 gene (MIM# 610865).
checks.explanation: Stated in the paragraph on Fowler syndrome.

checks.claim: Fowler syndrome presents with fetal akinesia deformation sequence, which differs from HDBSCC.
checks.evidence_quote: Clinically affected fetuses present with fetal akinesia deformation sequence with muscular neurogenic atrophy (Fowler et al., 1973) which is different from the clinical presentation of the cases in this report.

paragraphs.text: Mochida et al. (2010) studied affected members of a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts. In these patients they found a homozygous G-to-T transversion at the first base of intron 5 of the JAM3 gene (c.747+1G-T). RT-PCR of patient lymphoblastoid cells confirmed abnormal splicing, causing a frameshift with early termination. Akawi et al. (2013) described this mutation as c.612+1G-T (p.V205Lfs) using reference sequence NM_032801.4.

paragraphs.text: In a girl with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts, Akawi et al. paragraphs.text: In 2 affected brothers with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts, Akawi et al. (2013) identified a homozygous c.346G-A transition in exon 4 of the JAM3 gene, resulting in a glu116-to-lys (E116K) substitution in the Ig-like V-type domain. The brothers were born to nonconsanguineous parents of Afghani origin (family 2). The mutation segregated with the disease and was not found in dbSNP or the 1000 Genomes Project. In transfected HeLa cells, the mutant protein reached the plasma membrane normally. The authors suggested that the mutation may interfere with dimerization or with binding to interacting partners.

paragraphs.text: In a girl with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts, Akawi et al. (2013) identified a homozygous c.656G-A transition in exon 6 of the JAM3 gene, resulting in a cys219-to-tyr (C219Y) substitution in the Ig-like C2-type domain. The patient was born to Turkish parents who were second cousins (family 1). The mutation segregated with the disease and was not found in dbSNP or the 1000 Genomes Project. It was predicted to disrupt a disulfide bond. In transfected HeLa and COS-7 cells, the mutant protein was mostly retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and did not reach the plasma membrane, indicating a trafficking defect.

checks.evidence_quote: In family 1 we detected a non-synonomous mutation (c.656G>A) in exon 6 of JAM3 gene, which led to an amino acid substitution at position 219 (p.C219Y).
checks.explanation: The family 1 proband is a girl, and the mutation was homozygous.

checks.claim: The JAM3 c.656G-A transition results in a cys219-to-tyr (C219Y) substitution.

checks.evidence_quote: c.656G>A | p.C219Y | Homozygous | Non-synonomous | Ig-like C2-type

checks.evidence_quote: The parents of the affected child in this family are second cousins of Turkish origin.

checks.evidence_quote: the detected mutations segregated with disease status in the three families

checks.evidence_quote: The p.C219Y mutation detected in family 1 alters one of the four highly conserved cysteine residues of JAM3 disrupting one out of two disulfide bonds known to stabilize the Ig-folds of the protein.

checks.claim: In transfected HeLa and COS-7 cells, the JAM3 C219Y mutant protein was mostly retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and did not reach the plasma membrane.
checks.evidence_quote: comparison of the subcellular localization of flag-tagged C219Y mutants transiently expressed in HeLa (Figure 3; Supp. Figure S2A) and COS7 (Supp. Figure S2C) clearly showed that most of the mutated protein failed to reach the cell membrane
checks.explanation: Combined with the ER co-localization in HeLa cells. Strictly, the paper reports ER retention in HeLa cells, while in COS-7 cells it reports only failure to reach the membrane.
